lines.text: This is the engine on Boeing's new 777X. Its fan is three point four meters wide, the biggest ever on an airliner. So how does it push a plane?
It starts with the fan. Sixteen carbon fiber blades, swallowing tons of air every second.
But here's the trick. Most of that air never goes inside. About ten times more air flows around the core than through it.
The air that does go in hits the compressor. Row after row of spinning blades, each smaller than the last, squeezing it up to sixty times.
Then fuel sprays in and burns. The gas gets hotter than the melting point of the metal blades right behind it.
So those blades are coated in ceramic and covered in tiny holes, which blow a thin film of cooler air over the surface.
The hot blast spins the turbines. And shafts connect them to the compressor and the fan up front. The engine keeps itself spinning.
Hot gas shoots out the back, but most of the push comes from the fan air around it. Moving lots of air gently is what makes it efficient.
And like that fuel, your files can burn too. On Orbi Transfer, set a timer, and when it runs out, the file is gone for good.
